rv.q: What was once a spooky and balletic spectacle of 1980s excess, best known for the hit song “Memory” and purring chorines crawling on the seats, is now a glitter bomb of euphoric pandemonium.

After an already-legendary Off Broadway debut at the Perelman Arts Center in 2024, this production—under the chosen name Cats: The Jellicle Ball–has now re-inhabited Broadway, where it remains a categorical triumph.
You’d have to be a real stickler for tradition to begrudge Jellicle Ball its innovations, and one suspects even the stickliest will find joy in the tunes and story that remain in this show’s DNA.
This exhilarating Broadway production opened Tuesday at the Broadhurst Theater after its 2024 premiere at the Perelman Performing Arts Center in Lower Manhattan...
"Cats: The Jellicle Ball" just might become the next much-needed, must-see touring show from the House of Broadway.
As synth-powered entertainment, it’s exhilarating. As a display of loose-limbed fabulosity, it’s a marvel.
And yet, in placing new context and bodies inside the suit of ’80s excess, The Jellicle Ball reinvents it.
But the rest of the revisionist ball? A total blast from start to finish.
What those outsiders have achieved with The Jellicle Ball is a revival in the fullest sense of the word.
The result is a raucous, interactive, sensory overload.
It appears to me that Cats: The Jellicle Ball may become one of those legendary Broadway shows that someday you will tell others you were lucky enough to see.
The Jellicle Ball the must-see show of this or any season, and the bar against which revivals of canon shows should be measured against.
It is precisely all that history, deeply felt in this momentous staging, that makes both Moore and this production so otherworldly.
It's a transcendent, glitter-drenched revival that breaks all the rules of what Broadway can be – and in turn, creates something that is utterly extraordinary.
A spectacle of and about our time, Cats: The Jellicle Ball, sets an exciting new bar in theatrical artistry.
Not only is this Cats different from any you have ever seen before, it is the most dynamic musical show to be seen in New York right now.
The spectacle of Jellicle Ball is intoxicating for all who enter and give themselves over to the glamor.
This irresistible revival isn’t your grandma’s Cats; but in many ways, it is the truest version of the musical yet.
More than anything, Cats: The Jellicle Ball insists, through the hard-fought victory of Black and brown queer joy, that it's togetherness that gives all of us a reason for existence too.

That sense of joy saturates every aspect of the production, from Omari Wiles and Arturo Lyons’s exuberant, sinuous choreography to Qween Jean’s characteristically vivid costumes, a whimsical, scrumptious feast of bright color and texture that’s enhanced by Nikya Mathis’s hair and wig design.

CATS: The Jellicle Ball is an absolute trove of riches, filled with wonderful moments that bring together then and now while keeping everything fresh and alive, even for those totally unfamiliar with ballroom culture.
This one-of-a-kind, must-see extravaganza proves to be a most welcome tenant at the Broadhurst Theater.
If you hated Cats to begin with, I don’t know if this will cure you.

Artistically, the fresh interpretation not only offers the possibility of a renewed life and a new audience for this overly familiar 45-year-old show; it suggests how the art form as a whole can be reinvigorated.
Much improved from its 2024 incarnation, it nevertheless remains a curious cat, a problematic vintage musical transformed by a random (if cannily chosen) production concept.
When there’s dancing, the musical soars.
Cats: The Jellicle Ball is so fun even the Kittredges of the stuffy Upper East Side would give the show 10s across the board.
Both succeed gloriously because they trust their audiences to meet them where they are.
Reimagining Andrew Lloyd Webber’s “Cats” through the lens of Ballroom culture and voguing is brilliant.
Cats: The Jellicle Ball demonstrates what’s possible when a bold creative vision is brought to bear on weak material.

Reimagined by co-directors Zhailon Levingston and Bill Rauch, this electrifying production transforms T.S. Eliot’s poetic oddities into a full-throttle Harlem ballroom competition, where a 24-member ensemble struts, spins, and slays across categories like “Realness,” “Body,” and “Runway.”
The introduction of ballroom and 'house' culture breathes fresh energy and a human-scaled depth to the material.
Still, this is a Cats worth clawing for tickets over, and proof positive that Broadway can still turn a lewk.
I was impressed by the musical.
Swapping out cat ears for couture and the junkyard for the runway, this revival redefines itself and sharply recontextualizes the feline festival with a little less mystique and a lot more sparkle.
There is not enough glitter in the world to cover up how inane Cats truly is.
Cats: The Jellicle Ball is a fine tribute to ballroom.

cn.t: Critics hail this ballroom-reimagined Cats as a joyous, audacious triumph that rescues Lloyd Webber's divisive musical with spectacular choreography, dazzling costumes, and infectious energy—though a few find the opulence excessive.

vs.sum: One of Broadway's least comfortable theaters, with notoriously tight legroom and narrow seats. The lack of rake means tall patrons in front block your view. Restrooms are in the basement, creating long intermission lines. For legroom, target Row A or N in Orchestra.

acc.note: 6 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No steps from sidewalk. Infrared devices available.
